title: Cell structure
note: Every cell has a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes, and DNA. Prokaryotes keep their DNA in a nucleoid with no membrane around it. Eukaryotes add a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles; the endomembrane system (ER, Golgi, lysosomes, vesicles) makes, modifies, and ships proteins and lipids.

read.title: A protein's journey out of the cell
text: Imagine a cell in the pancreas making a digestive enzyme that must leave the cell. The instructions start in the nucleus, where the gene is copied into messenger RNA. The mRNA exits through a nuclear pore and meets a ribosome.

Because this protein is destined for export, its ribosome docks on the rough endoplasmic reticulum. As the chain grows, it threads into the ER interior, where it folds and often receives sugar groups. Small vesicles then bud off the ER and carry the protein to the Golgi apparatus.

The Golgi works like a shipping center. Its stacked sacs further modify the protein, then sort it and tag it for its destination. A vesicle carrying the finished enzyme pinches off, travels along microtubules, and fuses with the plasma membrane, releasing its contents outside the cell.

This route uses the endomembrane system, a set of membranes that are linked directly or by vesicles. It also includes lysosomes, which receive digestive enzymes by the same pathway. Mitochondria and chloroplasts are not part of it. They grow and divide on their own and carry their own DNA, clues that they began as bacteria living inside another cell.

q.q: Where does a protein destined for export begin to be made?
o: On a ribosome bound to the rough ER

q.q: What role does the Golgi play in this journey?
o: It copies the gene into mRNA
It modifies, sorts, and tags the protein

q.q: Why are mitochondria not counted in the endomembrane system?
o: They grow and divide on their own with their own DNA
